description:
We are a team brought together by a childhood fascination with space, science, and the mysteries of the universe. What started as curiosity and dreams of exploring beyond Earth has now become an opportunity to create something meaningful through the NASA Space Apps Challenge.

We aim to build an innovative, engaging, and scientifically grounded solution, following NASA's guidelines and using official datasets and resources.
summary:
Children are taught to admire rockets, but not the decisions that sustain the lives of those who crew them. That is the idea behind Solaris Horizont, an educational strategy and survival game where four explorers sustain a lunar mission through six modules: Energy, Life Support, Crops, Laboratory, Shelter and Telecommunications.

The project follows a simple rule: every decision counts. Players combine strategic planning with minigames and face solar crises based on NASA’s DONKI API. It also uses NASA data, including Moon Trek maps and JPL Horizons calculations. Players can explore the lunar surface and collect samples while facing solar radiation threats that endanger their survival and resources. Instead of fixed turns, the game progresses through missions and objectives assigned to each player, promoting cooperation and adaptation. As the challenge lasts longer, new obstacles and increasingly demanding situations arise.

It matters because, just as astronauts transmit science to Earth, this project brings it to children, who do not memorize data but experience and manage it. They discover that a mission depends on interconnected decisions and that exploring means learning what to choose and what to sacrifice.
details:
Lunar Guardians is an educational strategy and survival video game designed to help children and teenagers understand the decisions that sustain a space mission. Space content for young people tends either to oversimplify engineering or to make it too complex. Our game, by contrast, lets players live the reasoning behind a mission and not just its outcome.

How It Works

The player is the commander of a mission to the Moon. They lead four astronauts, drawn in a simple yet creative design and allocate energy, oxygen, water, food, and materials across six modules: Energy, Life Support, Crops, Laboratory, Shelter and Telecommunications. Rather than following a fixed turn-based structure, the game unfolds through missions and objectives assigned to each player. Added to this planning are minigames that push the player from deciding to acting, and a collaborative multiplayer mode for up to four players. Every decision has consequences: spending resources on research can delay repairs or compromise survival and solar crises, based on real records from NASA’s DONKI API, force players to choose what to protect first. Players can also venture onto the lunar surface to explore and collect scientific samples, facing solar radiation threats that can compromise their survival and mission resources. As players progress and spend more time in the challenge, they encounter additional obstacles and increasingly demanding situations that test their adaptability and strategic thinking. The ultimate goal is to care for the crew, produce and transmit science, repair the engine and confirm the rescue.

Key Benefits and Impact

  • It lets players grasp, without prior technical knowledge, that resources are limited and that a good decision rests on data.
  • It turns science into experience: players do not memorize that space is demanding; they find it out for themselves.
  • It adds practice to reflection through minigames.
  • It encourages teamwork: in the collaborative mode, players learn to argue, listen and correct course.
  • It brings NASA science closer to children and teenagers, as well as siblings, parents, and classmates, as a starting point for conversations about what was prioritized, what was lost and what would be done differently.

Tools and Technologies

  • JavaScript, HTML, and CSS: game development, with Canvas 2D to draw it.
  • Node.js: server.
  • Firebase: collaborative multiplayer mode.
  • NASA APIs (DONKI, Moon Trek, and JPL Horizons): data, maps and scientific information.
  • Playwright: automated testing.
  • Visual Studio Code: development environment.
  • Netlify: site hosting.

Creative Elements

  • It does not separate science from emotion: the astronauts are characters, and every choice matters because it affects someone.
  • It turns real NASA records into crises that players must solve.
  • It brings together strategy, minigames, exploration and cooperation in a single experience.

Factors We Considered

  • That the science be accurate yet understandable for children and teenagers.
  • That it teach without ceasing to be fun, because content that is boring, however rigorous, is neither played nor remembered.
  • Organizing the experience around missions and objectives to keep players engaged without overwhelming them.
  • Using everyday language and explaining technical terms in simple words.
  • Increasing the challenges progressively to maintain engagement and encourage strategic thinking.

Conclusion

With Solaris Horizont, we want the next time a child or teenager watches a rocket lift off, they also think about the people inside and the decisions that keep them alive. Exploring space demands science, but also judgment and that is the lesson this game aims to leave behind with every playthrough.
